```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Package versions are pinned via renv (see renv.lock); run renv::restore() to install.
# Functions are called with explicit pkg:: prefixes rather than attaching via library().

# Headline numbers used in the Summary. The price shock is written by the export-price-shock
# chunk below; the land-use results by r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R.
shock_2035 <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"))
lum <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_country_results.csv.gz"))

# Soybean oil's share of soybean crush value (Janzen & Wang 2025; see Methods). Must match
# SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE in r/land_use_model/01_prepare_data.R.
soy_oil_value_share <- 4.72 / (4.72 + 8.66)

# Additional forest loss relative to BAU: BAU stock minus scenario stock, so positive = more loss.
bau <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "bau") |>
  dplyr::select(country, year, carbon_bau = forest_carbon_tco2, area_bau = forest_area_ha)
loss <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_central", "vo_high", "vo_central_palm", "vo_central_soy")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(bau, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    carbon_loss = carbon_bau - forest_carbon_tco2, # t CO2
    area_loss = area_bau - forest_area_ha # ha
  )
global_loss <- loss |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(c(carbon_loss, area_loss, carbon_bau, area_bau), sum),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  )
gl <- function(scn, yr, var) global_loss[[var]][global_loss$scenario == scn & global_loss$year == yr]

final_year <- max(lum$year)
n_years <- final_year - min(lum$year)
country_final <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = carbon_loss / sum(carbon_loss), .by = scenario) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, dplyr::desc(carbon_loss))
central_final <- country_final |> dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_central")
# Countries whose additional loss peaks and then narrows by >5% (BAU later clears some of the
# same forest), among those with more than 1 Mt CO2 of additional loss.
gap_peaks <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_central") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    peak = max(carbon_loss),
    peak_year = year[which.max(carbon_loss)],
    final = carbon_loss[year == final_year],
    .by = country
  )
n_narrowing <- sum(gap_peaks$peak > 1e6 & gap_peaks$final < 0.95 * gap_peaks$peak)
mys <- gap_peaks[gap_peaks$country == "Malaysia", ]

# Crop attribution: palm-only and soy-only runs of the central shock. They sum to the joint run
# to within the interaction term reported here.
crop_split <- c(
  palm = gl("vo_central_palm", final_year, "carbon_loss"),
  soy = gl("vo_central_soy", final_year, "carbon_loss")
)
interaction_pct <- 100 * (gl("vo_central", final_year, "carbon_loss") - sum(crop_split)) /
  gl("vo_central", final_year, "carbon_loss")

fmt1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
fmt0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")

# Figures: one ggplot2 theme and one set of colors throughout. Scenarios and crops keep the same
# colors in every figure; magnitude on maps uses viridis, reversed so darker means more loss.
col_surface <- "#fcfcfb"
col_land <- "#ecebe6"
col_scenario <- c(Central = "#2a78d6", Sensitivity = "#eb6834")
col_crop <- c("Oil palm" = "#1baf7a", "Soybeans" = "#eda100")
map_ramp <- function(n) viridisLite::viridis(n, direction = -1)

theme_report <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = col_surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
theme_map <- function() {
  theme_report() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.justification = "center"
    )
}

# Country outlines (Natural Earth 1:110m), as vertices; see r/make_basemap.R.
basemap <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "natural_earth", "ne_110m_admin_0_countries.csv.gz"))
```

## Summary

These results are preliminary.

ICCT estimates that meeting the Net-Zero Framework's Base target at least cost would take about `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters of virgin vegetable oil a year for marine renewable diesel by 2035 [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. That is `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflower oil combined.

Using published supply and demand elasticities, that much extra demand raises vegetable-oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`% with the estimates from @chen2026 [Table S1 and Fig. 2B] and by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_high)`% with those from @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279]. Both numbers come from a linear approximation that works for small demand shifts, and this shift is large, so the exact percentages are rough. We use them to size the shock we feed into the land-use model, not as price forecasts.

The land-use model prices palm as palm oil but soybeans as whole beans. About 35% of the value of a crushed soybean is oil and the rest is meal [@janzen2025, Fig. 2], so if meal prices hold steady, a `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`% rise in the oil price raises the soybean price by about `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`%. The central scenario therefore raises palm oil prices `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`% and soybean prices `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`%.

With those prices, emLab's land-use model clears an extra `r fmt1(gl("vo_central", 2035, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha of forest in the first 15 years compared with business as usual, releasing `r fmt1(gl("vo_central", 2035, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. Over the model's full `r n_years`-year run the totals are `r fmt1(gl("vo_central", final_year, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha and `r fmt1(gl("vo_central", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂, or `r fmt1(gl("vo_high", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂ with the Roberts & Schlenker shock. The palm price increase causes `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the additional loss and the soybean increase `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. Most of it falls in a few countries: `r central_final$country[1]` and `r central_final$country[2]` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(central_final$share[1:2]))`%, and the top 12 countries for `r fmt0(100 * sum(central_final$share[1:12]))`%.

The next step is to turn this into an ILUC carbon intensity in g CO₂e/MJ, which can be compared with the 62 g CO₂e/MJ ICCT has used [@sturrup2026, p. 10] and the 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ that @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] estimate for palm.

## Background

### The IMO Net-Zero Framework

In April 2025 the International Maritime Organization approved draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI [@sturrup2026, p. 1] that would set binding greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) targets for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. GFI is measured in well-to-wake g CO₂e/MJ against a 2008 baseline of 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]. There are two targets. The Base target tightens from a 4% reduction in 2028 to 30% by 2035, and the stricter Direct Compliance target from 17% to 43%. Ships above the Base target pay \$380 per tonne of excess CO₂e (Tier 2), and ships between the two targets pay \$100 per tonne (Tier 1) [@seber2025, pp. 1–2]. The adoption vote planned for October 2025 was postponed by at least a year [@sturrup2026, p. 1].

Fuels are judged only on their direct life-cycle emissions, with nothing for land-use change. Blending in biofuel costs less than the \$380 Tier 2 penalty, so the cheapest strategy is to blend just enough to meet the Base target. In ICCT's least-cost fuel mix, used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) runs out at about 5% of shipping energy, and virgin vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) covers the rest, reaching 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

| Fuel | Life-cycle carbon intensity (g CO₂e/MJ) |
|---|---|
| 2008 baseline | 93.3 |
| Heavy fuel oil (HFO) | 92.8 |
| Fossil LNG | 85.7 |
| Soy vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) | 42.3 |
| Soy FAME biodiesel | 35.7 |
| Used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) | 13.1 |

: Direct life-cycle carbon intensities used by ICCT: 2008 baseline (p. 1); fossil LNG, 85.65 (p. 2); HFO, 92.78, soy VO-RD, soy FAME (35.74) and UCO-RD (p. 6) [@seber2025]. None include indirect land-use change.

### Indirect land-use change

Indirect land-use change (ILUC) happens when demand for a biofuel feedstock raises crop prices and the higher prices lead to forest being cleared for farmland somewhere else. These emissions fall outside the fuel's own supply chain, so a fuel mix can meet the GFI targets on paper while adding emissions that nobody counts. The steps in this analysis:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["IMO Net-Zero Framework"] --> F["Marine VO-RD demand<br/><i>ICCT cost-optimization</i>"]
  F --> B["Virgin vegetable-oil demand<br/><i>1.22 kg oil per kg RD</i>"]
  B --> C["Vegetable-oil price shock<br/><i>this report</i>"]
  C --> D["Forest loss by country<br/><i>emLab land-use model</i>"]
  D --> E["ILUC carbon intensity<br/><i>next step</i>"]
```

ICCT converts renewable diesel to oil at 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel [@seber2025, p. 3, note 9].

Published ILUC estimates for vegetable-oil biofuels range widely:

| Source | Approach | ILUC result |
|---|---|---|
| ICCT climate & revenue brief [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11] | Fixed factor applied to ICCT's demand projection | 62 g CO₂e/MJ; ~285 Mt CO₂e/yr by 2035; ~950 Mt CO₂e over 2028–2035 |
| U.S. EPA model comparison [@epa2023mce, Table 7.7-1, p. 113] | Five models, soybean-oil biodiesel shock | Land-use change: 10 to 295 kg CO₂e/MMBTU (GCAM: 62) |
| @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] | Econometric estimates of demand → price → deforestation for palm, 2002–2018 | 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ (90% CI 48.7–113.5) |
| GLOBIOM for the EU [@valin2015, p. x] | Global economic land-use model, emissions spread over 20 years | 231 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil, 150 for soybean oil |

: ICCT takes its 62 from the EPA model comparison [@sturrup2026, p. 10]. The only 62 in the EPA's results table is GCAM's land-use-change value, which is in kg CO₂e/MMBTU (≈ 59 g CO₂e/MJ), so we assume that is the source. With it, ICCT finds the ILUC-adjusted fleet GFI reaches 93.86 g CO₂e/MJ by 2035, above the fossil baseline [@sturrup2026, Table A1, p. 15].

Like Chen et al., we estimate how much the demand shift raises prices and then use an econometric land-use model to translate prices into forest loss, instead of assuming an ILUC factor.

## Methods and assumptions

The analysis has four steps:

1. Convert ICCT's 2035 vegetable-oil demand into a price shock.
2. Translate that shock into prices for the crops in emLab's land-use model.
3. Run the model with baseline and shocked prices, both at a zero carbon price, and take the difference in forest loss.
4. Express the additional emissions per MJ of fuel. This step is not done yet.

### From demand to a price shock {#sec-price-shock}

When demand shifts out, the equilibrium price rises by roughly the size of the shift divided by the difference between the supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, panel C, p. 2279]:

$$ \%\Delta P \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{D}{Q_0}}_{\text{demand shift}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_d}}_{\text{multiplier } M} $$

where $D$ is marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, $Q_0$ is baseline world production, $\varepsilon_s > 0$ is the supply elasticity and $\varepsilon_d < 0$ is the demand elasticity.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, 2035 ($D$) | 139.3 billion L | ICCT [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5] |
| Baseline market ($Q_0$) | ≈ 204 Mt: world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflowerseed oil, 2024/25 | USDA PSD [@usdapsd] |
| Oil density, to put $D$ and $Q_0$ in the same units | 0.92 kg/L | ICCT's own soy-oil conversion: 12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L (0.919 kg/L) [@seber2025, Table A1, p. 7] |
| Demand elasticity, central ($\varepsilon_d$) | −0.284, the inverse of a demand flexibility of −3.523 (SE 1.085) | @chen2026 [Table S1, col. 3] |
| Supply elasticity, central ($\varepsilon_s$) | ≈ 0.12: long-run 0.10 for palm and 0.13 for competing oil crops, weighted by production | @chen2026 [Fig. 2B, rows 3–4, p. 4] |
| Elasticities, sensitivity | $\varepsilon_s = 0.10$, $\varepsilon_d = -0.05$ | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279] (ranges 0.09–0.12 and −0.03 to −0.07) |
| Demand year | 2035 only | Our choice: the final year of the ICCT projection |
| "Beyond marginal" flag | demand share > 25% | Our own cutoff for where the approximation gets unreliable (not from a source) |

: Inputs to the price shock. The central multiplier is $M \approx 2.5$; the sensitivity, $M \approx 6.7$.

Some notes on these choices:

- Vegetable oils substitute for one another, so we treat them as one market even though the marine demand is for soy oil [@chen2026, p. 4]. $Q_0$ covers the same four oils as the Chen elasticities.
- We keep the supply elasticity in the multiplier. The land-use model takes prices as given, so the price we give it should already reflect the supply response. Leaving $\varepsilon_s$ out ($M \approx 3.5$) would raise the shock by about 40%. This assumes the land-use model's own supply response is roughly in line with $\varepsilon_s \approx 0.12$, which we have not checked.
- The formula is a first-order approximation, and from about 2032 marine demand is a large share of the market, so the 2035 shock gives the scale of the effect, not its exact size. Roberts & Schlenker also note that because the multiplier is a convex function of the elasticities, its expected value is higher than the value at the point estimates [@roberts2013, p. 2280], which points the same way.
- Both sets of elasticities are long-run. Oil palm takes about four years to start fruiting, so supply barely responds in the short run [@chen2026, p. 4].
- Crushing soybeans also produces meal, and meal revenue offsets some of the pressure on oil prices. Roberts & Schlenker cut their price effect by a third when a third of the calories come back as animal feed [@roberts2013, p. 2280]. We make no adjustment like this to the oil price, so on this count the shock is too high. (Meal does affect how the shock reaches the soybean price; see the next section.)
- The formula reproduces both source papers' headline price effects (see [Results](#sec-results-price)).

### Mapping the shock to the model's crops {#sec-mapping}

Following @chen2026 [p. 3], we apply the same percentage shock to all vegetable-oil prices. They find that palm oil prices respond to production shocks in competing oil crops about as strongly as to shocks in palm itself (their Fig. 2A, p. 4), and that the four oil prices move together in the long run, with cointegrating coefficients close to one (soybean 1.04, canola 1.01, sunflower 0.86) [@chen2026, Table S5]. Other work points the same way but adds detail: in an equilibrium model of world vegetable-oil markets, @cui2017 [abstract] find that soy oil diverted to US biodiesel is replaced mostly by palm oil, and @santeramo2017 [p. 13] estimates cross-price elasticities between individual oils and finds a mix of substitutes and complements that varies by oil and region. Oil-specific pass-through would be a reasonable refinement.

Of the land-use model's 17 crops, only two produce vegetable oil: `Oil, palm`, priced per tonne of palm oil, and `Soybeans`, priced per tonne of beans. According to a comment in upstream's `00c_run_cobweb.R` (Section 5), the model's baseline prices are observed 2020 prices: \$768/t for palm and \$415/t for soybeans. Both are within 2% of the World Bank's 2020 averages for palm oil (\$752/t) and soybeans (\$407/t). Soybean oil averaged \$838/t that year [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1].

| Model crop | Shock | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palm oil | $\%\Delta P$ | The model prices palm as oil | — |
| Soybeans | $s \times \%\Delta P$, with $s = 0.353$ | Oil is only part of a soybean's value, and we hold the meal price fixed. $s = \$4.72 / (\$4.72 + \$8.66)$, from the 2007–2025 average per-bushel values of soybean oil and meal | @janzen2025 [Fig. 2] (USDA AMS Illinois plant prices; 11 lb oil and 48 lb meal per bushel) |
| Rapeseed/canola, sunflower | not modeled | Not among the model's crops | — |

: How the oil-price shock enters the land-use model.

Two checks on $s$: Irwin's 2007–2017 averages (\$4.43 oil, \$8.33 meal) give 0.347 [@irwin2017, Fig. 3], and World Bank 2020 prices for soybean oil and meal (\$838/t and \$394/t) give 0.33 [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1]. The share moves around a lot week to week. It stayed between 25% and 35% over 2013–2020, has rarely been below 35% since, and briefly hit 50% in 2021 and 2025 [@janzen2025, Fig. 3]. It is an accounting share and says nothing about how soybean prices actually respond.

Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, so their land-use response is missing and ILUC is understated. We still define $Q_0$ over all four oils, since that is the market the Chen elasticities describe; using palm and soy alone would inflate the demand share. In 2024/25, 86% of world rapeseed came from Canada, the EU, China, India, Australia and Russia, and 90% of sunflowerseed from Russia, Ukraine, the EU, Argentina, Kazakhstan and China [@usdapsd], so most of the missing response is probably outside tropical forests. We have not quantified it.

### The land-use model {#sec-land-use-model}

We use emLab's global deforestation model (`emlab-ucsb/land-based-solutions`), copied into this repository. [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) lists every change we made to it.

The model is a fractional logit (fixest, quasibinomial) of each grid cell's annual deforestation rate on potential agricultural revenue and the remaining share of tree cover, with cell and country-by-year fixed effects. It is estimated on 2001–2020 (29.1 million cell-years). A cell's revenue is crop price minus transport cost, times attainable yield, summed over the 17 crops using each crop's harvested share as weights and capitalized at 5%. Transport cost scales with travel time to port and the crude-oil price.

Starting from 2020 tree cover, the model steps forward one year at a time from 2021 to 2171 over 1,450,769 cells in 154 countries. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and cleared forest never grows back.

All runs use a zero carbon price. BAU uses 2020 prices. The central run raises palm oil prices by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_central)`%, and the sensitivity run by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_high)`% and `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_high)`%. Two more runs apply the central shock to palm and to soybeans separately, so the loss can be split by crop. Prices jump once, in the first model year, and stay there, so model year 2035 means 15 years after the shock rather than the calendar year.

Forest carbon (t CO₂) is tree cover times carbon density, and forest area (ha) is forest carbon divided by carbon density, using the model's own conversion. We count forest carbon lost as emissions, which leaves out peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration. As a sanity check, the model has `r fmt0(sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 2020, `r fmt0(100 * sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 4.06e9)`% of FAO's 4.06 billion ha [@fao2020fra, p. 1]; the two use different definitions of forest.

### ILUC carbon intensity (not done yet)

The last step will divide the additional emissions by the energy in the fuel, giving g CO₂e/MJ that can be added to VO-RD's direct 42.3 g CO₂e/MJ [@seber2025, p. 6]. Because the model works at the cell level, the result will break down by country.

## Data

### ICCT demand projection

ICCT's Table 1 (p. 5) gives the least-cost fuel mix for 2028–2035 [@seber2025]. We read it straight from the PDF.

```{r}
#| label: scrape-icct-table-1

pdf_path <- file.path(
  "data",
  "icct_biofuel_demand_report",
  "ID-450-Vegetable-Oil_research-brief_final.pdf"
)

# Extract page 5 as text and keep only the data rows (years 2028–2035)
page5 <- pdftools::pdf_text(pdf_path)[5]
lines <- stringr::str_trim(stringr::str_split(page5, "\n")[[1]])
data_lines <- stringr::str_subset(lines, "^20(2[89]|3[0-5])\\b")

# Each data row yields exactly 10 numeric tokens:
#   year, shipping demand, base target, fossil LNG %,
#   UCO-RD %, UCO-RD bl, VO-RD %, VO-RD bl, UCO demand bl, VO demand bl
nums <- stringr::str_extract_all(data_lines, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")
mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[seq_len(10)])))

icct_table_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
names(icct_table_1) <- c(
  "year",
  "shipping_energy_demand_ej",
  "base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj",
  "fossil_lng_pct",
  "ucord_pct_energy_demand",
  "ucord_billion_liters",
  "vord_pct_energy_demand",
  "vord_billion_liters",
  "uco_demand_billion_liters",
  "vo_demand_billion_liters"
)

icct_table_1 <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

knitr::kable(
  icct_table_1 |>
    dplyr::select(
      year,
      shipping_energy_demand_ej,
      base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj,
      ucord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_billion_liters,
      vo_demand_billion_liters
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Shipping energy (EJ)",
    "Base target (g CO₂e/MJ)",
    "UCO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD fuel (billion L)",
    "Virgin VO feedstock (billion L)"
  ),
  caption = "ICCT Table 1, selected columns [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, the last column, is the demand shock D."
)
```

### Baseline vegetable-oil production

$Q_0$ is world production of the four oils in 2024/25, summed across countries from the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service's PSD oilseeds data (`data/usda_psd_oilseeds/psd_oilseeds_csv.zip`, downloaded 2026-07-31) [@usdapsd]. USDA revises PSD continuously, so a later download may give slightly different numbers.

```{r}
#| label: psd-q0

psd_zip_path <- file.path("data", "usda_psd_oilseeds", "psd_oilseeds_csv.zip")
psd <- utils::read.csv(unz(psd_zip_path, "psd_oilseeds.csv"))

q0_market_year <- 2024 # marketing year 2024/25

psd_four_oils <- psd |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Commodity_Description %in%
      c("Oil, Palm", "Oil, Soybean", "Oil, Rapeseed", "Oil, Sunflowerseed"),
    Attribute_Description == "Production",
    Market_Year == q0_market_year
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    production_mt = sum(Value) / 1000, # reported in 1000 MT
    .by = Commodity_Description
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(production_mt))

knitr::kable(
  psd_four_oils,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Commodity", "World production, 2024/25 (million t)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "World production of the four major vegetable oils (USDA PSD). Total: ",
    round(sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt), 1),
    " million t."
  )
)
```

### Land-use model inputs and outputs

The model inputs are emLab's `land-based-solutions` data on Nextcloud (`data/parallelized/1_input/full`), which we read but never modify. The simulation outputs (about 7 GB) are not in the repository; `r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R` reduces them to country × scenario × year totals (`data/derived/land_use_country_results.csv.gz`) and 0.5° grid-square totals (`data/derived/land_use_grid_loss.csv.gz`), which this report reads. Map outlines are Natural Earth's 1:110m countries [@naturalearth], stored as plain coordinates by `r/make_basemap.R`.

## Results

### Vegetable-oil price shock {#sec-results-price}

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-parameters

# Q0: world production of the four oils (psd_four_oils), converted to billion liters at
# 0.92 kg/L, ICCT's own soy-oil conversion (12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L, ICCT Table A1).
q0_mt <- sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt) # ~204 Mt
oil_density_kg_l <- 0.92
q0_billion_liters <- q0_mt / oil_density_kg_l # ~221 billion L

# Central elasticities (Chen et al. 2026). Demand: flexibility of -3.523 (Table S1 col 3)
# inverts to eps_d = -0.284. Supply: long-run 0.10 (palm) and 0.13 (competing oil crops)
# (Fig. 2B rows 3-4), weighted by production share as in their eps_S formula.
demand_flexibility_chen <- -3.523
eps_d_chen <- 1 / demand_flexibility_chen
share_palm <- psd_four_oils$production_mt[
  psd_four_oils$Commodity_Description == "Oil, Palm"
] /
  q0_mt
eps_s_chen <- 0.10 * share_palm + 0.13 * (1 - share_palm)

# Sensitivity: Roberts & Schlenker (2013) staple-food elasticities (Table 1).
eps_s_rs <- 0.10
eps_d_rs <- -0.05

# eps_d is negative, so the multiplier denominator is eps_s + |eps_d|.
m_chen <- 1 / (eps_s_chen - eps_d_chen) # ~2.5
m_rs <- 1 / (eps_s_rs - eps_d_rs) # ~6.7

# Check: each multiplier should recover its source paper's own headline price effect.
validation <- tibble::tribble(
  ~check                                                        , ~shock_pct , ~m     , ~reported                                  ,
  "Chen et al. (p. 3): biofuels used 8.5% of vegetable oil, 2002-2018" , 8.5 , m_chen , "21.2% (90% CI: 12.2-28.5%) (p. 3)" ,
  "Roberts & Schlenker (p. 2277): ethanol mandate = 5% of world calories" , 5.0 , m_rs , "about 30% (p. 2280); 5% x their Table 1 multipliers gives 29-39%"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(implied_pct = round(shock_pct * m, 1)) |>
  dplyr::select(check, shock_pct, implied_pct, reported)

knitr::kable(
  validation,
  col.names = c(
    "Check",
    "Demand shift (% of market)",
    "Implied %ΔP (our formula)",
    "Paper's result"
  ),
  caption = paste0(
    "Multipliers: central M = ", round(m_chen, 2), " (Chen et al.), sensitivity M = ",
    round(m_rs, 2), " (Roberts & Schlenker). Both recover their source's headline result."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: derive-price-shock

# %ΔP_t = (D_t / Q0) * M, expressed as a percent. beyond_marginal flags years where the shift
# exceeds 25% of the market, outside the regime where the approximation is reliable.
price_shock <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    vo_demand_billion_liters,
    demand_share_pct = 100 * vo_demand_billion_liters / q0_billion_liters,
    pct_delta_p_central = demand_share_pct * m_chen,
    pct_delta_p_high = demand_share_pct * m_rs,
    beyond_marginal = demand_share_pct > 25
  )

knitr::kable(
  price_shock |>
    dplyr::mutate(beyond_marginal = ifelse(beyond_marginal, "yes", "")),
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "VO demand (billion L)",
    "Share of market (%)",
    "%ΔP, central",
    "%ΔP, sensitivity",
    "Beyond marginal"
  ),
  caption = "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand. Years marked 'beyond marginal' are outside the range where the linear approximation holds up."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

price_shock_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "Central", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_central),
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "Sensitivity", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_high)
)

scenario_labels <- c(Central = "Central (Chen et al.)", Sensitivity = "Sensitivity (Roberts & Schlenker)")

ggplot2::ggplot(price_shock_long, ggplot2::aes(year, pct, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.8, stroke = 0.8, colour = col_surface) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_scenario, labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_scenario, labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = price_shock$year) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in vegetable-oil price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

The land-use runs use the 2035 values.

```{r}
# vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv.
handoff_2035 <- price_shock |> dplyr::filter(year == 2035)

dir.create(file.path("data", "derived"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
utils::write.csv(

utils::write.csv(

cat(sprintf(
```

### Forest loss {#sec-results-forest}

Additional loss is the difference between forest in the BAU run and in a shocked run. It is cumulative, so the value in the last model year is the total additional loss over the whole simulation.

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-global

horizons <- c(2035, 2050, final_year)
global_table <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% horizons) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year),
    carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9,
    area_mha = area_loss / 1e6,
    pct_of_bau_carbon = 100 * carbon_loss / carbon_bau
  )

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = global_table$years_after_shock[global_table$scenario == "vo_central"],
    "Central: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_central"],
    "Central: Mha" = global_table$area_mha[global_table$scenario == "vo_central"],
    "Central: % of BAU forest carbon" = global_table$pct_of_bau_carbon[global_table$scenario == "vo_central"],
    "Sensitivity: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_high"],
    "Sensitivity: Mha" = global_table$area_mha[global_table$scenario == "vo_high"],
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU, all countries."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

global_ts <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_central", "vo_high")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year),
    scenario = ifelse(scenario == "vo_central", "Central", "Sensitivity"),
    carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(global_ts, ggplot2::aes(years_after_shock, carbon_gt, colour = scenario)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_scenario, labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 25), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Cumulative additional forest carbon loss relative to BAU",
    x = "Years after the price shock",
    y = expression("Gt CO"[2])
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

About half of the full-run loss in the central scenario (`r fmt0(100 * gl("vo_central", 2035, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_central", final_year, "carbon_loss"))`%) happens in the first 15 years.

#### By country and crop

To split the loss by crop, we ran the central shock on palm alone and on soybeans alone. Palm accounts for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the additional loss and soybeans for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. The two single-crop runs add up to the combined run to within `r formatC(abs(interaction_pct), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, so the interaction between them is negligible.

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-country-chart
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.2

top_n <- 12
top_countries <- central_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]
other_label <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(central_final$carbon_loss > 0) - top_n)

crop_by_country <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_central_palm", "vo_central_soy")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = ifelse(country %in% top_countries, country, other_label),
    crop = ifelse(scenario == "vo_central_palm", "Oil palm", "Soybeans")
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(carbon_loss) / 1e6, .by = c(label, crop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(c(top_countries, other_label))))
bar_totals <- crop_by_country |> dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(mt), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(crop_by_country, ggplot2::aes(mt, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE), # palm first, from zero
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = bar_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt0(mt)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Additional forest carbon loss by country and crop",
    subtitle = "Central scenario, full horizon",
    x = expression("Mt CO"[2]),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-country-table

country_table <- country_final |>

by_scenario <- function(scn, ...) {

}
country_table <- by_scenario("vo_central", carbon_loss, area_loss, area_bau, share) |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_central_palm", carbon_palm = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_central_soy", carbon_soy = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(by_scenario("vo_high", carbon_high = carbon_loss), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    country,
    carbon_mt = carbon_loss / 1e6,
    palm_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_palm, 0) / 1e6,
    soy_mt = dplyr::coalesce(carbon_soy, 0) / 1e6,
    area_kha = area_loss / 1e3,
    share_pct = 100 * share,
    pct_of_bau_area = 100 * area_loss / area_bau,

  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(carbon_mt))

DT::datatable(
  country_table,
  rownames = FALSE,
  colnames = c(
    "Country",
    "Central: Mt CO₂",
    "of which palm",
    "of which soybeans",
    "Central: thousand ha",
    "Central: share of total (%)",
    "Central: % of country's BAU forest",
    "Sensitivity: Mt CO₂"
  ),
  caption = "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU over the full horizon, by country. Palm and soybean columns are the single-crop runs.",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
) |>
  DT::formatRound(c("carbon_mt", "palm_mt", "soy_mt", "area_kha", "share_pct", "pct_of_bau_area", "carbon_mt_high"), digits = 1)
```

`r sum(central_final$carbon_loss > 0)` countries lose some additional forest, but `r central_final$country[1]`, `r central_final$country[2]` and `r central_final$country[3]` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(central_final$share[1:3]))`% of the total. Only cells that grow oil palm or soybeans respond, because those are the only prices that change.

Because cleared forest never grows back, BAU can later clear forest that a shocked run cleared earlier. In Malaysia the additional loss peaks at `r fmt0(mys$peak / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ in model year `r mys$peak_year` and falls to `r fmt0(mys$final / 1e6)` Mt CO₂ by `r final_year`, and `r n_narrowing` countries drop more than 5% below their peak. Globally the additional loss is still rising at the end of the run. The ILUC calculation will need to handle this timing.

## Caveats and next steps

Next steps:

- Express the additional emissions as an ILUC carbon intensity (g CO₂e/MJ), with a breakdown by country.
- Compare our copy of the model with upstream (snippet in `r/land_use_model/PROVENANCE.md`), which has been refactored since we copied it on 31 July 2026.

What the estimates leave out or assume:

- Only forest carbon is counted. Peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration are not. Peat was 614 of the 1,086 Tg CO₂e in Chen et al.'s estimate [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13], so this matters most for Indonesia and Malaysia. This understates ILUC.
- Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, which also understates ILUC.
- The price shock comes from a linear approximation applied to a very large demand shift (63% of the market). The true price response is probably larger.
- The soybean price change uses an accounting share (0.353), not an estimated market response.
- We make no adjustment for soy meal in the oil-price shock, which overstates it.
- The price step assumes a supply elasticity of about 0.12. We have not checked whether the land-use model's own supply response matches.
- Prices jump once in the first model year and stay there, and cleared forest never grows back (see [Methods](#sec-land-use-model)).

## Appendix A: Changes to the land-use model code {#sec-lum-changes}

This lists every change we made to the emLab land-use model to run the price scenarios, for the model's authors to review. Starting point: upstream `emlab-ucsb/land-based-solutions`, `r/robert_test/parallelization/` at commit `e207c2b` (31 July 2026), copied to `r/land_use_model/` (see `r/land_use_model/PROVENANCE.md`). Anything not listed here is unchanged.

**Unchanged:** `simulation_functions.R` (including `update_revenues()` and `simulate_10_dt()`), `packages.R`, `r/directories.R` (now only read from, via `paths.R`), the deforestation model and its coefficients, and the fixed-effect construction (pixel FEs, the 2016–2020 country-year FE window, asymmetric-information FEs).

**All scripts**

1. `r/robert_test/parallelization/` → `r/land_use_model/` in every `here::here()` path.

**New file: `paths.R`**

2. Defines the input root `input_wdir`, read via `r/directories.R` as `{data_directory}/parallelized` and treated as read-only, and the output root `wdir`, the repo's git-ignored `land_use_model_runs/`. It stops if `wdir` is inside any Nextcloud folder or inside the inputs. This is so our outputs can't sync over the shared Nextcloud files of the same name.

**`01_prepare_data.R`**

3. Carbon price fixed at 0: `CP_LIST` (10 carbon prices) replaced by `CP <- 0`.
4. New input `PRICE_SHOCKS` (Section 1): % price change per shocked crop, one element per scenario, with `bau` first and unshocked. Scenarios: `bau`; `vo_20pct` (smoke test, `Oil, palm` and `Soybeans` both +20%); `vo_central` and `vo_high`, built from the 2035 shocks read from `data/derived/vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv` (`pct_delta_p_central`, `pct_delta_p_high`), with `Oil, palm` taking the full shock and `Soybeans` taking `SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE` (0.353, Janzen & Wang 2025) of it; and `vo_central_palm` and `vo_central_soy`, the central shock applied to one crop at a time, for crop attribution. Sources for every number are in [Methods](#sec-mapping).
5. New Section 2b: expands `PRICE_SHOCKS` into `PRICE_SCENARIOS`, one full 17-crop price vector per scenario, starting from the `CPrice == 0` rows of `final_prices_allcp`. Writes `price_scenarios.csv`. Stops if a shocked crop isn't in the model, or if any crop in `endo_input_data` has no price.
6. Section 6: `update_revenues()` runs once per price scenario (`revenue_<scenario>` columns) instead of once per carbon price (`revenue_cp<P>`). BAU revenue is computed the same way instead of being taken from `data_past$revenue`, so every scenario uses one formula. The two BAU versions agree to ~1e-12, and the script prints that check on every run.
7. Section 8: chunk files carry `revenue_<scenario>` columns in place of `revenue_cp0` and `revenue_cp<P>`.
8. Section 8: the per-pixel attributes file `grid_smry.csv` also carries `lat` and `lon`, for mapping.
9. Section 11: `model_params.rds` stores `cp` and `price_scenarios` in place of `cp_list`.
10. Paths come from `paths.R` instead of the hard-coded `/Users/rheilmayr/Nextcloud/...` `wdir`, which upstream used for both inputs and outputs.

**`02_run_simulations.R`**

11. The 38 distinct simulations (56 labeled blocks across endog/exog, fi/fi_bl_vp/ai_bl_vp and carbon price) are replaced by one `simulate_10_dt()` run per price scenario, at `cp = 0` with `pixel_fe`. This is the same construction as upstream's `endog_fi_blvp` runs, $D(0, V(P))$, with scenario prices in place of carbon-price equilibrium prices.
12. Output parquet columns are `scn, pixel_id, year, biomass` (upstream: `crp_price, cprice, pixel_id, year, info, biomass`). The row-count check is now pixels × scenarios × years.
13. Paths come from `paths.R`, as in `01`.

**Disabled scripts**

14. `00_generate_sample_data.R`, `00c_run_cobweb.R`, `01b_prepare_uncertainty_draws.R`, `02b_run_simulations_uncertainty.R`, and `03_aggregate_results.R` through `09_conceptual_diagrams.R` (including `03b`) have a `stop()` as their first line. They still expect upstream's carbon-price outputs and use upstream's hard-coded paths, which on a colleague's machine point at the shared Nextcloud folder. `00` and `00c` write into `1_input/` itself. Each `stop()` comes out only when that script is adapted to `paths.R`.

**New file: `03_summarise_results.R`**

15. Reduces `02`'s per-pixel results to two files for the report, pairing each result file with its chunk file for each pixel's `country` and `CF`:
    - `data/derived/land_use_country_results.csv.gz`: country × scenario × year totals of forest carbon (`sum(biomass)`, t CO₂) and forest area (`sum(biomass / CF)`, ha, using upstream's `ha_per_pixel = CF_pix / CF`).
    - `data/derived/land_use_grid_loss.csv.gz`: per 0.5° grid square (from `grid_smry.csv` coordinates), 2020 forest carbon and final-year additional loss relative to BAU for each scenario.

    Stops if BAU 2020 forest carbon doesn't match `01`'s `grid_smry.csv`, or if any scenario's gridded loss doesn't sum to its country-level loss.

**`run_pipeline.R`**

16. `STAGES` runs `01` → `02` → `03_summarise_results.R`; upstream stages `03`–`07` are commented out.

**Verification** (200-pixel sample inputs, `1_input/smpl`):

- BAU emissions per pixel, annualized the same way as `03`'s `bl_emit_co2_y`, match upstream's reference run (`5_validation/sim_results_exog_ref_smpl.csv`) to within 0.003% for all 201 pixels.
- `vo_20pct` biomass is never higher than BAU, and is lower in the 110 of 201 pixels that grow palm or soy.

**Verification** (full inputs, `1_input/full`, 1,450,769 pixels):

- BAU revenue recomputed with `update_revenues()` matches upstream's `data_past$revenue` to within 7e-12.
- At every pixel, final-year (2171) biomass is never higher under a shock than under BAU, and never higher under `vo_high` than under `vo_central`. The shocks affect 711,420 pixels, those with a palm or soybean harvest share.
- `vo_central_palm` and `vo_central_soy` sum to `vo_central` to within 0.04% of its additional loss, 15 years after the shock and at the end of the horizon.
- `03_summarise_results.R`: BAU 2020 forest carbon summed by country equals `01`'s per-pixel 2020 biomass, and each scenario's gridded loss equals its country-level loss.
- Runtime on a 64 GB laptop, six scenarios: `01` 241 s (peak memory ~27 GB), `02` 145 s, `03_summarise_results.R` 43 s.

## Appendix B: Results of the +20% test run {#sec-test-run}

This is the first run the model's authors asked for: oil palm and soybean prices both up 20% (soybeans by the full 20%, without the oil-share adjustment), at a zero carbon price, with everything else as in [Methods](#sec-land-use-model). It is a check on how the model responds, not a policy scenario.

```{r}
#| label: test-run-global

test_global <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_20pct")) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    carbon = sum(forest_carbon_tco2),
    area = sum(forest_area_ha),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, year)
test_bau <- test_global[test_global$scenario == "bau", ]
test_shock <- test_global[test_global$scenario == "vo_20pct", ]
stopifnot(identical(test_bau$year, test_shock$year))

base_year <- min(lum$year)
test_rows <- match(c(base_year + 1, 2035, 2050, final_year), test_bau$year)
bau_loss <- test_bau$carbon[test_bau$year == base_year] - test_bau$carbon[test_rows]
extra_loss <- test_bau$carbon[test_rows] - test_shock$carbon[test_rows]

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = test_bau$year[test_rows] - base_year,
    "BAU forest carbon loss (Gt CO₂)" = bau_loss / 1e9,
    "Additional loss, +20% (Gt CO₂)" = extra_loss / 1e9,
    "Additional loss, +20% (Mha)" = (test_bau$area[test_rows] - test_shock$area[test_rows]) / 1e6,
    "Additional as % of BAU loss" = 100 * extra_loss / bau_loss,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = c(0, 1, 3, 2, 2),
  caption = "+20% test run: cumulative forest carbon loss under BAU and additional loss from the price increase, all countries."
)
```

BAU loses `r fmt1(bau_loss[1] / 1e9)` Gt CO₂ of forest carbon in the first year, close to the ~4.2 Gt first-year figure noted in a comment in upstream's `01_prepare_data.R` (Section 5). The 20% price increase adds `r fmt1(100 * extra_loss[2] / bau_loss[2])`% to BAU's cumulative loss over 15 years. That share shrinks over longer horizons because BAU loss keeps accumulating while the extra loss from the shock levels off.

```{r}
#| label: test-run-countries

test_countries <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("bau", "vo_20pct"), year %in% c(2035, final_year)) |>
  dplyr::select(country, scenario, year, forest_carbon_tco2) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    extra_mt = (forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "bau"] - forest_carbon_tco2[scenario == "vo_20pct"]) / 1e6,
    .by = c(country, year)
  )
test_top <- dplyr::inner_join(
  test_countries |> dplyr::filter(year == 2035) |> dplyr::select(country, extra_15 = extra_mt),
  test_countries |> dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |> dplyr::select(country, extra_full = extra_mt),
  by = "country"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share_pct = 100 * extra_full / sum(extra_full)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(extra_full)) |>
  utils::head(10)

knitr::kable(
  test_top,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Country", "Additional loss, 15 years (Mt CO₂)", "Additional loss, full horizon (Mt CO₂)", "Share of global (%)"),
  caption = "+20% test run: the ten countries with the largest additional forest carbon loss."
)
```
